Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember. Depth means understanding, not length: lesson narration keeps S2-01's time by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never drop or compress away what the book teaches to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, the book's content is complete. Lesson narration has a time target (S2-01), met by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-06] BIE is the link between the learner and the book, like a teacher (Navin, 24 October 2026). The book is the base; BIE carries its text, easy or hard, into the learner's mind. Never just read the line out: every book line is opened (what its words mean, why it is so, where it is seen, what follows), at the depth of the level profile.
[G-07] Two layers, like a film (Navin, 24 October 2026). The writer layer (understanding, plan, script) decides what is said and how deep, following the level profile and the book's own level. The presentation layer (director, video blocks, render) is the same skilled quality for every learner, from class 6 to postgraduate; only the detail shown follows the level, never the craft.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

How BIE talks to you: every request is a task card (JSON) followed by its source. The card names the unit, its parts with their content type and required questions, the ids of the rules above that apply, the output, the ids you must cover and the context. The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.
For a read_page card:
- card.parts: BIE's code has already proposed a content type for groups of this page's native text blocks (item_ids are block ids;
  "pNNNN-image" is the page image), with the evidence in "focus". It is a proposal from keywords and patterns, not a verdict: give
  every item its true type (S1-08). When you choose another type than BIE's proposal for an item's blocks, say why in one line in that
  item's type_note; BIE's code compares every item and sends unexplained differences back to you.
- card.coverage: every id in must_cover must be in some item's block_ids or in boilerplate_block_ids; may_skip lists blocks BIE thinks are
  running headers or page numbers. Never list an id that is not on this page.
- card.context.before and after: one line from the previous and the next page, for context only.
How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part, a type you chose against BIE's proposal) with a reason each,
  and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "". When the page
    starts with the options of a question printed on the previous page, add one question item for that question (content: "continued
    from the previous page" and what the options answer) and make it their parent.
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the card.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree). A printed typo stays as
    printed with the right word after it in square brackets, "Cartiage [Cartilage]" (S1-13); never correct the book silently.
  - content_type: one of BIE's nine type ids above, by what the content is. An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a table
    row or a diagram label usually takes its table's or diagram's type. "none" only for a question, an answer option or an item that is
    not teachable.
  - type_note: "" when you agree with BIE's proposal for this item's blocks (or there is none); otherwise one line on why your type fits.
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside"; one answer, one basis: an answer that
    would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one "book" and one "outside" (S1-14). BIE's code
    checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how", at least the required questions of its content type, and no answer that only
    repeats its question or the item's words.
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
  - unpack: how a teacher opens this book line for the learner (S1-15; BIE is the link between the learner and the book, never a
    reader of the line). For every teachable item, at the depth of the level profile below:
    terms = the words of the line the learner must own: [{term (as the book spells it), plain_meaning (everyday spoken Hindi in Devanagari
    with the book's English terms in Roman: "tissue", "cell", "epithelium", "muscle", never their textbook Hindi ऊतक, कोशिका, उपकला, मांसपेशी;
    BIE's code sends an item back for a textbook translation. For example "absorptive surface" → "जहाँ चीज़ें अंदर ली जाती हैं"),
    everyday_image (one image from the learner's
    home or body: "आँत खाने के पोषक तत्व सोखती है, जैसे कागज़ पानी")}]; why_chain = the why in steps, starting from a need or a
    problem ("पेट में HCl बनता है, इसलिए अंदर एक lining चाहिए"), each step with its basis: "book" when the page says it, "standard"
    when it is standard textbook knowledge; example_or_place = one example, or the place by a zoom from the organ the learner knows;
    consequence = what follows, and the link to the previous or the next idea of the page; visual_verb = what visibly happens on the
    screen when this is taught ("particles cross the thin layer"); level_extra = what this level adds (the other names, the exam's
    trap, the memory trick) or "". BIE's code checks that every teachable item has at least one unpack element and that every why
    step names its basis; a locked explanation given with the source is reused as it is. A question item or a pure heading leaves
    unpack empty.
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.
- text_image_disagreements: where the text layer and the image differ.
Reply with the JSON object only.

Level profile: UPSC / State PCS (level_profiles.json; learners: UPSC and State PCS aspirants, often from arts backgrounds, who need understanding more than technical vocabulary).
- Terms: fewer technical terms: only the ones the exam asks, each opened with its plain meaning and an everyday image; a term the exam never asks is explained in words, not named.
- Why: 2 step(s); a two-step why from a need the learner can feel, then its link to daily life, health or governance.
- Where found: the main places, each linked to something the learner already knows (a disease, a food, a news item).
- Exam beats: the PYQ pattern: how this fact has been asked (statement combinations, 'which is correct', odd one out) and the wording that traps.
- Links: daily life, health, the news and earlier chapters of the same paper.

How real teachers open a book line (teacher example bank 2026-10-24.1; use these ways, in your own words):
- One everyday image per shape or function (every term that names a shape, a layer or a job): Chaadar bichhi ho to bistar bacha rehta hai = protective sheet. Cube wala game, har side barabar = cuboidal. Building ka pillar = columnar. Farsh ki tiles = squamous, isliye tessellated bhi kehte hain.
- The word root where it helps (a term whose parts carry its meaning): Epi yaani upar; epithelium yaani upar ki parat. Slender yaani long aur narrow.
- Why starts from a need (every why step): Pet mein HCl banta hai, isliye andar ek lining chahiye jo khud na jale. Cells bahar ki taraf hain, tootne ka chance zyada, isliye regeneration zyada.
- Link to something already known (a new place or a new structure): Peritoneum, jaise lungs ke aas-paas pleura aur heart ke aas-paas pericardium: wahi kaam, pet ke andar.
- Meaning with two or three real examples (an abstract word in the book): Sensory perception yaani pehchanna: thanda lagna, dard hona, pressure mehsoos karna.
- Open the book's adjective (Navin's example) (a book line names a kind of surface, job or place without saying what it is): Book: 'epithelium absorptive aur secretive surfaces par milta hai'. Teacher: absorptive surface yaani jahan cheezein andar li jaati hain, jaise aant khane ke poshak tatva sokhti hai; secretive yaani jahan cells kuch bana kar bahar chhodte hain, jaise glands enzyme ya juice. Aur epithelium wahan kyon? Kyunki ek patli, lagi hui parat hi cheezon ko paar jaane de sakti hai aur bana kar chhod sakti hai.

p0003-b0002 | There are mainly four different types of tissues present in our body.
p0003-b0003 | 1. Epithelial- provides covering or lining
p0003-b0004 | 2. Muscular- helps in movement
p0003-b0005 | 3. Neural- responds to stimuli
p0003-b0006 | 4. Connective- supports, links and cushions
p0003-b0007 |  Epithelium covers most organs and cavities within the body.
p0003-b0008 |  It also forms a barrier to keep different body systems separate.
p0003-b0009 |  Epithelial tissue cells are tightly packed and form a continuous sheet.
p0003-b0010 |  They have only a small amount of cementing material between them and
p0003-b0011 | almost no intercellular spaces.

items.content:
There are mainly four different types of tissues present in our body.
1. Epithelial- provides covering or lining
2. Muscular- helps in movement
3. Neural- responds to stimuli
4. Connective- supports, links and cushions

teacher_understanding.question: Which four tissue groups does the page identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: Epithelial, muscular, neural and connective tissues are the four main groups identified.

teacher_understanding.question: How do their principal functions differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: Epithelial tissue covers or lines; muscular tissue enables movement; neural tissue responds to stimuli; connective tissue supports, links and cushions.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does a body need different tissue groups?
teacher_understanding.answer: A protective boundary, movement, rapid responses and physical support involve different tasks. Groups of specialised cells divide these tasks rather than requiring one cell type to perform them equally well.

prerequisites: tissue as a group of cells performing a shared function
items.exam_note: Core tissue–function matching and odd-one-out material; these are main groups, not epithelial subtypes.

Specialised cell groups divide these jobs, making tissue classification useful.

unpack.example_or_place: Connect a covering to skin, movement to bending an arm, and a response to touching something hot.
unpack.consequence: The rest of the page zooms into the covering-and-lining group.

items.content: Epithelium covers most organs and cavities within the body.

teacher_understanding.question: What spatial role does epithelium have?
teacher_understanding.answer: It forms a covering or lining associated with most organs and body cavities.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the page later give examples of epithelial linings?
teacher_understanding.answer: Examples include blood vessels, lung air sacs, kidney tubules, the digestive tract and the mouth.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a lining important at these surfaces?
teacher_understanding.answer: A surface separates one environment from another. A lining can protect the underlying body while regulating exchange across that boundary.

items.exam_note: Epithelium is not restricted to the outside of the body.

why_chain.step: Organs and cavities have surfaces that meet other spaces or materials.
Epithelium covers or lines these surfaces.

unpack.example_or_place: Follow swallowed food into the digestive tract and identify its inner lining.
unpack.consequence: Covering is a position; the particular lining may additionally absorb, secrete or protect.
unpack.visual_verb: Trace a continuous inner surface.
unpack.level_extra: Distinguish covering an organ from making up the whole organ.

items.content: It also forms a barrier to keep different body systems separate.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the page describe epithelium as a barrier?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its barrier role helps keep different body systems separate rather than leaving their contents in unrestricted contact.

teacher_understanding.question: How can a barrier still allow useful exchange?
teacher_understanding.answer: A biological barrier need not be an impermeable wall. Depending on the epithelial type, materials can cross through controlled routes while the tissue maintains a boundary.

items.exam_note: Barrier does not mean that absorption, secretion or diffusion cannot occur.

why_chain.step: Different body compartments need to remain distinct.
Epithelium provides a separating barrier.

unpack.example_or_place: An intestinal lining separates the contents of the gut from underlying tissues.
unpack.consequence: A continuous sheet is suited to separating spaces.
unpack.visual_verb: Separate two compartments with a sheet.
unpack.level_extra: Avoid the absolute claim that epithelial barriers block every substance.

items.content: Epithelial tissue cells are tightly packed and form a continuous sheet.

teacher_understanding.question: How are epithelial cells arranged?
teacher_understanding.answer: Closely adjoining cells collectively form a continuous sheet rather than a loose scattering.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is this sheet arrangement used?
teacher_understanding.answer: In the epithelial coverings and linings of organs and cavities described on the page.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does close packing suit a barrier?
teacher_understanding.answer: Large uncontrolled gaps would interrupt the boundary. Close cell contact helps a lining maintain continuity.

items.exam_note: Closely packed cells are a distinguishing epithelial feature.

why_chain.step: A boundary needs coverage without large breaks.
Tightly packed epithelial cells form a continuous sheet.

unpack.example_or_place: Zoom into the mouth lining from a whole surface to adjoining cells.
unpack.consequence: Cell packing supports the barrier role introduced above.
unpack.visual_verb: Fit cells edge to edge.
unpack.level_extra: Link organisation to function rather than memorising 'tightly packed' alone.

items.content: They have only a small amount of cementing material between them and almost no intercellular spaces.

teacher_understanding.question: What occupies the space between adjacent epithelial cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page describes little cementing material and almost no spaces between neighbouring cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What does 'intercellular' locate?
teacher_understanding.answer: It means between cells, not inside a cell.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this detail reinforce the continuous-sheet description?
teacher_understanding.answer: When neighbouring cells lie very close together, cells themselves occupy most of the sheet, with little intervening material.

items.exam_note: Retain 'almost no' rather than turning it into an absolute zero.

unpack.example_or_place: An enlarged section through an epithelial sheet.
unpack.consequence: The tissue is cell-rich rather than dominated by material between cells.
unpack.visual_verb: Zoom into the narrow gap between cells.
unpack.level_extra: Do not confuse intercellular with intracellular.

items.content: All epithelium is usually separated from the underlying tissue by an extracellular fibrous basement membrane.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the supporting boundary described below epithelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page identifies an extracellular, fibrous basement membrane between epithelium and underlying tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the basement membrane lie?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lies beneath the epithelial layer, at its interface with the underlying tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a supporting layer useful here?
teacher_understanding.answer: An epithelial sheet needs anchorage. The basement membrane helps support and attach it to the tissue beneath.

teacher_understanding.question: How is a basement membrane different from a cell membrane?
teacher_understanding.answer: A basement membrane is extracellular supporting material beneath a tissue; a cell membrane encloses an individual cell.

items.exam_note: Position and extracellular nature are important; do not identify it as the cell's own membrane.

why_chain.step: A surface sheet needs a stable base.
A basement membrane underlies and supports epithelial attachment.

unpack.example_or_place: Show a side section of lining, basement membrane and underlying tissue.
unpack.consequence: The epithelial sheet is distinct from, but attached to, what lies below it.
unpack.visual_verb: Lift the sheet to reveal its base.
unpack.level_extra: Preserve the printed 'All ... usually' wording without teaching an unnecessary absolute.

items.content: Epithelial cells often acquire additional specialisation as gland cells, which can secrete substances at the epithelial surface. Sometimes a portion of the epithelial tissue folds inward, and a multicellular gland is formed. This is glandular epithelium.

teacher_understanding.question: What additional role can epithelial cells acquire?
teacher_understanding.answer: They can specialise as gland cells that release substances at an epithelial surface.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the page describe formation of a multicellular gland?
teacher_understanding.answer: A portion of an epithelial sheet folds inward, producing a gland made of multiple cells.

teacher_understanding.question: When is the inward-folding route described?
teacher_understanding.answer: It occurs sometimes when epithelial tissue forms a multicellular gland; the page does not present it as the fate of every epithelial sheet.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is secretion a specialisation beyond simple covering?
teacher_understanding.answer: Secretory cells produce and release useful substances, so they do an active manufacturing-and-release job in addition to occupying a surface.

items.exam_note: Understand glandular epithelium as a functional specialisation; multicellular means many cells.

why_chain.step: Body surfaces need useful substances such as lubricating secretions.
Epithelial cells can specialise for secretion, and a folded portion can form a multicellular gland.

unpack.example_or_place: Use saliva in the mouth to make secretion tangible.
unpack.consequence: Epithelium is not merely a passive covering.
unpack.visual_verb: Fold the sheet inward and release droplets.
unpack.level_extra: Do not treat every epithelial cell as a gland cell or every gland as multicellular.

teacher_understanding.answer: It contrasts the shapes and layering of squamous, stratified squamous, cuboidal and ciliated columnar epithelia.

teacher_understanding.question: Which visual features should a learner inspect first?
teacher_understanding.answer: Inspect the number of cell layers, the shape of surface cells and the projections on the columnar surface.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a side view help identify these tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: A top view alone can hide cell height and multiple layers. A side view reveals whether cells are flattened, cube-like, tall or stacked.

items.exam_note: Useful for identifying tissue by morphology rather than label recall.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Simple squamous | Location: Blood vessel lining, capillaries, air sac lining of lungs, Bowman’s capsule of kidney | Structure: A single layer of flat cells having irregular boundaries | Function: Transport by diffusion and where minimal protection is required

teacher_understanding.question: What arrangement defines simple squamous epithelium here?
teacher_understanding.answer: One layer of flat cells with irregular boundaries creates a thin lining.

teacher_understanding.question: Which locations must be associated with it?
teacher_understanding.answer: Blood-vessel lining, capillaries, lung air-sac lining and Bowman’s capsule of the kidney.

teacher_understanding.question: What function does the table associate with this thin layer?
teacher_understanding.answer: Transport by diffusion and use where protection requirements are minimal.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does a thin single layer favour diffusion?
teacher_understanding.answer: Diffusing particles have a short distance to cross. At lung air sacs, a thin barrier helps gases move between air and blood.

teacher_understanding.question: How is this different from stratified squamous epithelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: Simple squamous has one flat-cell layer and is associated with diffusion; stratified squamous has multiple layers and is associated with protection.

items.exam_note: High-value location–shape–function matching; one layer favours exchange rather than heavy abrasion resistance.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Simple Cuboidal Epithelium | Location: The tubular lining of kidneys, glandular ducts | Structure: A single layer of short cylindrical cells. It may have microvilli as in proximal convoluted tubules | Function: Absorption and secretion

teacher_understanding.question: What structure does the table describe?
teacher_understanding.answer: A single layer, described in the book as short cylindrical cells, sometimes with microvilli, as in proximal convoluted tubules.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is simple cuboidal epithelium found according to this row?
teacher_understanding.answer: In kidney tubular lining and glandular ducts.

teacher_understanding.question: Which two functions are paired here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Absorption and secretion: taking substances in and releasing substances.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the shape wording be understood?
teacher_understanding.answer: Conventionally, cuboidal cells are roughly as tall as wide, as the illustration suggests. 'Short cylindrical' is the book's wording, not a reason to identify them as tall columnar cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can microvilli help absorption in kidney tubules?
teacher_understanding.answer: Microvilli increase the surface available for exchange. Kidney tubules reclaim useful substances from the fluid passing through them.

items.exam_note: Kidney tubules, microvilli and absorption–secretion are key associations. Microvilli are not cilia.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Simple Columnar Epithelium | Location: Digestive tract and upper respiratory tract lining | Structure: A single layer of columnar cells (tall and slender) and often ciliated | Function: Protection, absorption, mucus secretion and movement in a specific direction

teacher_understanding.question: What does columnar mean in this row?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cells are tall and slender and are arranged in a single layer; the row also describes them as often ciliated.

teacher_understanding.question: Which locations are listed?
teacher_understanding.answer: The digestive tract and upper respiratory tract lining.

teacher_understanding.question: What functions are listed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Protection, absorption, mucus secretion and movement in a specific direction.

teacher_understanding.question: How can cilia produce directional movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their coordinated beating moves material over the epithelial surface, such as mucus carrying trapped particles.

teacher_understanding.question: Should all these locations and functions be assigned to every columnar lining?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Many digestive columnar linings are non-ciliated, and much of the upper respiratory lining is pseudostratified ciliated columnar. Shape, ciliation and number of layers must be checked separately.

items.exam_note: Avoid 'all columnar cells are ciliated'. The book's location statement is broad and the table continues with pseudostratified tissue.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Stratified Squamous Epithelium | Location: The lining of the mouth and vagina | Structure: Made up of several layers of cells, continuously sloughed off and regenerated. The older layer of cells is pushed upwards and becomes flat. The lower layer is columnar and metabolically active | Function: Protection

teacher_understanding.question: How are the cell layers arranged and renewed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Several layers are present. A lower columnar, metabolically active layer lies below older cells that move upwards and flatten; surface cells are shed and replaced.

teacher_understanding.question: Which protective linings are listed?
teacher_understanding.answer: The mouth and vagina.

teacher_understanding.question: Why do several layers suit these locations?
teacher_understanding.answer: These surfaces experience friction. Multiple layers allow superficial wear without immediately exposing the deeper tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does regeneration maintain protection?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cell division in the deeper layer supplies replacements as older surface cells are lost, maintaining the barrier despite wear.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is it squamous even though the lower layer is columnar?
teacher_understanding.answer: Stratified epithelial types are named by the surface-cell shape; flat upper cells determine the squamous designation.

items.exam_note: High-value trap: not every cell in stratified squamous tissue is flat.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Stratified Cuboidal | Location: Mammary glands, sweat gland and salivary glands | Structure: The upper layer is cuboid and other layers may be cuboidal or other types | Function: Protection of ducts of various glands

teacher_understanding.question: What cell arrangement identifies stratified cuboidal epithelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: There are multiple layers, with cuboid cells in the upper layer; deeper layers may be cuboidal or of other types.

teacher_understanding.question: Which glands are associated with it?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mammary glands, sweat gland and salivary glands are listed, with protection of gland ducts as the function.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is the duct distinction important?
teacher_understanding.answer: A gland contains secretory regions and channels carrying the secretion. Naming a tissue in its ducts does not mean that the entire gland has the same lining.

teacher_understanding.question: How does stratification relate to its stated role?
teacher_understanding.answer: Additional cell layers strengthen a duct's protective lining compared with a single-layer arrangement.

items.exam_note: Associate with gland ducts; surface cuboidal shape does not require every deeper layer to be identical.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Stratified Columnar | Location: Male urethra and lobar ducts of salivary glands | Structure: There is a layer of columnar cells present on squamous, columnar or cuboidal epithelial cells | Function: Protection and secretion

teacher_understanding.question: What makes this epithelium stratified columnar?
teacher_understanding.answer: A columnar cell layer lies above other epithelial cells, which the page says may be squamous, columnar or cuboidal.

teacher_understanding.question: Which locations are given?
teacher_understanding.answer: The male urethra and lobar ducts of salivary glands.

teacher_understanding.question: Which functions are paired?
teacher_understanding.answer: Protection and secretion.

teacher_understanding.question: How should it be distinguished from simple columnar tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Simple columnar has one cell layer. Stratified columnar has surface columnar cells above additional cells, so layer count must be checked as well as shape.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should 'male urethra' not become a claim about its entire length?
teacher_understanding.answer: Epithelial linings can change along a passage. Stratified columnar occurs in parts of the male urethra, not as a uniform lining of every part.

items.exam_note: Location matching is important. Urethra is not ureter; stratified is not pseudostratified.

teacher_understanding.question: What arrangement defines simple squamous epithelium here?
teacher_understanding.answer: One layer of flat cells with irregular boundaries creates a thin lining.

teacher_understanding.question: Which locations must be associated with it?
teacher_understanding.answer: Blood-vessel lining, capillaries, lung air-sac lining and Bowman’s capsule of the kidney.

teacher_understanding.question: What function does the table associate with this thin layer?
teacher_understanding.answer: Transport by diffusion and use where protection requirements are minimal.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does a thin single layer favour diffusion?
teacher_understanding.answer: Diffusing particles have a short distance to cross. At lung air sacs, a thin barrier helps gases move between air and blood.

teacher_understanding.question: How is this different from stratified squamous epithelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: Simple squamous has one flat-cell layer and is associated with diffusion; stratified squamous has multiple layers and is associated with protection.

replace_items.exam_note: High-value location–shape–function matching; one layer favours exchange rather than heavy abrasion resistance.

output.page_summary: Four principal tissue groups have different jobs. Epithelium forms closely packed coverings and linings supported by a basement membrane and can specialise into glands. Six epithelial types are compared through their cell arrangement, locations and functions, with four accompanying illustrations.

items.content:
There are mainly four different types of tissues present in our body.
1. Epithelial- provides covering or lining
2. Muscular- helps in movement
3. Neural- responds to stimuli
4. Connective- supports, links and cushions

teacher_understanding.question: Which four tissue groups does the page identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: Epithelial, muscular, neural and connective tissues are the four main groups identified.

teacher_understanding.question: How do their principal functions differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: Epithelial tissue covers or lines; muscular tissue enables movement; neural tissue responds to stimuli; connective tissue supports, links and cushions.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does a body need different tissue groups?
teacher_understanding.answer: A protective boundary, movement, rapid responses and physical support involve different tasks. Groups of specialised cells divide these tasks rather than requiring one cell type to perform them equally well.

prerequisites: tissue as a group of cells performing a shared function
items.exam_note: Core tissue–function matching and odd-one-out material; these are main groups, not epithelial subtypes.

items.content: Epithelium covers most organs and cavities within the body.

teacher_understanding.question: What spatial role does epithelium have?
teacher_understanding.answer: It forms a covering or lining associated with most organs and body cavities.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the page later give examples of epithelial linings?
teacher_understanding.answer: Examples include blood vessels, lung air sacs, kidney tubules, the digestive tract and the mouth.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a lining important at these surfaces?
teacher_understanding.answer: A surface separates one environment from another. A lining can protect the underlying body while regulating exchange across that boundary.

items.exam_note: Epithelium is not restricted to the outside of the body.

why_chain.step: Organs and cavities have surfaces that meet other spaces or materials.
Epithelium covers or lines these surfaces.

unpack.example_or_place: Follow swallowed food into the digestive tract and identify its inner lining.
unpack.consequence: Covering is a position; the particular lining may additionally absorb, secrete or protect.
unpack.visual_verb: Trace a continuous inner surface.
unpack.level_extra: Distinguish covering an organ from making up the whole organ.

items.content: It also forms a barrier to keep different body systems separate.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the page describe epithelium as a barrier?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its barrier role helps keep different body systems separate rather than leaving their contents in unrestricted contact.

teacher_understanding.question: How can a barrier still allow useful exchange?
teacher_understanding.answer: A biological barrier need not be an impermeable wall. Depending on the epithelial type, materials can cross through controlled routes while the tissue maintains a boundary.

items.exam_note: Barrier does not mean that absorption, secretion or diffusion cannot occur.

why_chain.step: Different body compartments need to remain distinct.
Epithelium provides a separating barrier.

unpack.example_or_place: An intestinal lining separates the contents of the gut from underlying tissues.
unpack.consequence: A continuous sheet is suited to separating spaces.
unpack.visual_verb: Separate two compartments with a sheet.
unpack.level_extra: Avoid the absolute claim that epithelial barriers block every substance.

items.content: Epithelial tissue cells are tightly packed and form a continuous sheet.

teacher_understanding.question: How are epithelial cells arranged?
teacher_understanding.answer: Closely adjoining cells collectively form a continuous sheet rather than a loose scattering.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is this sheet arrangement used?
teacher_understanding.answer: In the epithelial coverings and linings of organs and cavities described on the page.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does close packing suit a barrier?
teacher_understanding.answer: Large uncontrolled gaps would interrupt the boundary. Close cell contact helps a lining maintain continuity.

items.exam_note: Closely packed cells are a distinguishing epithelial feature.

unpack.example_or_place: Zoom into the mouth lining from a whole surface to adjoining cells.
unpack.consequence: Cell packing supports the barrier role introduced above.
unpack.visual_verb: Fit cells edge to edge.
unpack.level_extra: Link organisation to function rather than memorising 'tightly packed' alone.

teacher_understanding.question: What occupies the space between adjacent epithelial cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page describes little cementing material and almost no spaces between neighbouring cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What does 'intercellular' locate?
teacher_understanding.answer: It means between cells, not inside a cell.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this detail reinforce the continuous-sheet description?
teacher_understanding.answer: When neighbouring cells lie very close together, cells themselves occupy most of the sheet, with little intervening material.

items.exam_note: Retain 'almost no' rather than turning it into an absolute zero.

items.content: All epithelium is usually separated from the underlying tissue by an extracellular fibrous basement membrane.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the supporting boundary described below epithelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page identifies an extracellular, fibrous basement membrane between epithelium and underlying tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the basement membrane lie?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lies beneath the epithelial layer, at its interface with the underlying tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a supporting layer useful here?
teacher_understanding.answer: An epithelial sheet needs anchorage. The basement membrane helps support and attach it to the tissue beneath.

teacher_understanding.question: How is a basement membrane different from a cell membrane?
teacher_understanding.answer: A basement membrane is extracellular supporting material beneath a tissue; a cell membrane encloses an individual cell.

items.exam_note: Position and extracellular nature are important; do not identify it as the cell's own membrane.

unpack.consequence: The epithelial sheet is distinct from, but attached to, what lies below it.

items.content: Epithelial cells often acquire additional specialisation as gland cells, which can secrete substances at the epithelial surface. Sometimes a portion of the epithelial tissue folds inward, and a multicellular gland is formed. This is glandular epithelium.

teacher_understanding.question: What additional role can epithelial cells acquire?
teacher_understanding.answer: They can specialise as gland cells that release substances at an epithelial surface.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the page describe formation of a multicellular gland?
teacher_understanding.answer: A portion of an epithelial sheet folds inward, producing a gland made of multiple cells.

teacher_understanding.question: When is the inward-folding route described?
teacher_understanding.answer: It occurs sometimes when epithelial tissue forms a multicellular gland; the page does not present it as the fate of every epithelial sheet.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is secretion a specialisation beyond simple covering?
teacher_understanding.answer: Secretory cells produce and release useful substances, so they do an active manufacturing-and-release job in addition to occupying a surface.

items.exam_note: Understand glandular epithelium as a functional specialisation; multicellular means many cells.

teacher_understanding.answer: Inspect the number of cell layers, the shape of surface cells and the projections on the columnar surface.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a side view help identify these tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: A top view alone can hide cell height and multiple layers. A side view reveals whether cells are flattened, cube-like, tall or stacked.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Simple squamous | Location: Blood vessel lining, capillaries, air sac lining of lungs, Bowman’s capsule of kidney | Structure: A single layer of flat cells having irregular boundaries | Function: Transport by diffusion and where minimal protection is required

teacher_understanding.question: What arrangement defines simple squamous epithelium here?
teacher_understanding.answer: One layer of flat cells with irregular boundaries creates a thin lining.

teacher_understanding.question: Which locations must be associated with it?
teacher_understanding.answer: Blood-vessel lining, capillaries, lung air-sac lining and Bowman’s capsule of the kidney.

teacher_understanding.question: What function does the table associate with this thin layer?
teacher_understanding.answer: Transport by diffusion and use where protection requirements are minimal.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does a thin single layer favour diffusion?
teacher_understanding.answer: Diffusing particles have a short distance to cross. At lung air sacs, a thin barrier helps gases move between air and blood.

teacher_understanding.question: How is this different from stratified squamous epithelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: Simple squamous has one flat-cell layer and is associated with diffusion; stratified squamous has multiple layers and is associated with protection.

items.exam_note: High-value location–shape–function matching; one layer favours exchange rather than heavy abrasion resistance.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Simple Cuboidal Epithelium | Location: The tubular lining of kidneys, glandular ducts | Structure: A single layer of short cylindrical cells. It may have microvilli as in proximal convoluted tubules | Function: Absorption and secretion

teacher_understanding.question: What structure does the table describe?
teacher_understanding.answer: A single layer, described in the book as short cylindrical cells, sometimes with microvilli, as in proximal convoluted tubules.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is simple cuboidal epithelium found according to this row?
teacher_understanding.answer: In kidney tubular lining and glandular ducts.

teacher_understanding.question: Which two functions are paired here?
teacher_understanding.answer: Absorption and secretion: taking substances in and releasing substances.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the shape wording be understood?
teacher_understanding.answer: Conventionally, cuboidal cells are roughly as tall as wide, as the illustration suggests. 'Short cylindrical' is the book's wording, not a reason to identify them as tall columnar cells.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can microvilli help absorption in kidney tubules?
teacher_understanding.answer: Microvilli increase the surface available for exchange. Kidney tubules reclaim useful substances from the fluid passing through them.

items.exam_note: Kidney tubules, microvilli and absorption–secretion are key associations. Microvilli are not cilia.

why_chain.step: Kidney tubules need to recover useful substances from tubular fluid.
An absorptive lining with microvilli provides more surface for this exchange.

unpack.example_or_place: Zoom into a kidney tubule rather than the kidney's filtering capsule.
unpack.consequence: Different parts of the same organ can have different epithelial types.
unpack.visual_verb: Enlarge the surface with tiny projections and move substances across.
unpack.level_extra: Microvilli mainly increase surface area; cilia mainly move material along a surface.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Simple Columnar Epithelium | Location: Digestive tract and upper respiratory tract lining | Structure: A single layer of columnar cells (tall and slender) and often ciliated | Function: Protection, absorption, mucus secretion and movement in a specific direction

teacher_understanding.question: What does columnar mean in this row?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cells are tall and slender and are arranged in a single layer; the row also describes them as often ciliated.

teacher_understanding.question: Which locations are listed?
teacher_understanding.answer: The digestive tract and upper respiratory tract lining.

teacher_understanding.question: What functions are listed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Protection, absorption, mucus secretion and movement in a specific direction.

teacher_understanding.question: How can cilia produce directional movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Their coordinated beating moves material over the epithelial surface, such as mucus carrying trapped particles.

teacher_understanding.question: Should all these locations and functions be assigned to every columnar lining?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Many digestive columnar linings are non-ciliated, and much of the upper respiratory lining is pseudostratified ciliated columnar. Shape, ciliation and number of layers must be checked separately.

items.exam_note: Avoid 'all columnar cells are ciliated'. The book's location statement is broad and the table continues with pseudostratified tissue.

Absorptive specialisations and, where present, beating cilia meet these different needs.

unpack.example_or_place: Link food absorption to the intestine and mucus clearance to air passages.
unpack.consequence: One shape category can carry different surface specialisations and jobs.
unpack.visual_verb: Raise tall cells, release mucus and sweep it along.
unpack.level_extra: Keep columnar shape distinct from ciliated surface and pseudostratified arrangement.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Stratified Squamous Epithelium | Location: The lining of the mouth and vagina | Structure: Made up of several layers of cells, continuously sloughed off and regenerated. The older layer of cells is pushed upwards and becomes flat. The lower layer is columnar and metabolically active | Function: Protection

teacher_understanding.question: How are the cell layers arranged and renewed?
teacher_understanding.answer: Several layers are present. A lower columnar, metabolically active layer lies below older cells that move upwards and flatten; surface cells are shed and replaced.

teacher_understanding.question: Which protective linings are listed?
teacher_understanding.answer: The mouth and vagina.

teacher_understanding.question: Why do several layers suit these locations?
teacher_understanding.answer: These surfaces experience friction. Multiple layers allow superficial wear without immediately exposing the deeper tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does regeneration maintain protection?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cell division in the deeper layer supplies replacements as older surface cells are lost, maintaining the barrier despite wear.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is it squamous even though the lower layer is columnar?
teacher_understanding.answer: Stratified epithelial types are named by the surface-cell shape; flat upper cells determine the squamous designation.

items.exam_note: High-value trap: not every cell in stratified squamous tissue is flat.

why_chain.step: Friction can wear away cells on exposed linings.
Several layers and replacement from below maintain protection as surface cells are lost.

unpack.example_or_place: Feel food rubbing against the inner cheek to understand why mouth lining needs protection.
unpack.consequence: Protection depends on both layering and renewal, not simply on flat shape.
unpack.visual_verb: Push new cells upward, flatten them and shed the top cells.
unpack.level_extra: Compare simple squamous exchange with stratified squamous protection.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Stratified Cuboidal | Location: Mammary glands, sweat gland and salivary glands | Structure: The upper layer is cuboid and other layers may be cuboidal or other types | Function: Protection of ducts of various glands

teacher_understanding.question: What cell arrangement identifies stratified cuboidal epithelium?
teacher_understanding.answer: There are multiple layers, with cuboid cells in the upper layer; deeper layers may be cuboidal or of other types.

teacher_understanding.question: Which glands are associated with it?
teacher_understanding.answer: Mammary glands, sweat gland and salivary glands are listed, with protection of gland ducts as the function.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is the duct distinction important?
teacher_understanding.answer: A gland contains secretory regions and channels carrying the secretion. Naming a tissue in its ducts does not mean that the entire gland has the same lining.

teacher_understanding.question: How does stratification relate to its stated role?
teacher_understanding.answer: Additional cell layers strengthen a duct's protective lining compared with a single-layer arrangement.

items.exam_note: Associate with gland ducts; surface cuboidal shape does not require every deeper layer to be identical.

why_chain.step: A gland's secretion needs a protected passage to travel through.
Stratified cuboidal epithelium protects ducts of various glands.

unpack.example_or_place: Follow sweat from its gland through the duct towards the skin surface.
unpack.consequence: The same cuboidal shape can occur in single-layer absorptive tissue or multilayered protective ducts.
unpack.visual_verb: Wrap a gland duct in layered cube-like cells.
unpack.level_extra: Contrast simple cuboidal kidney tubules with stratified cuboidal gland ducts.

items.content: Types of Epithelial Tissue: Stratified Columnar | Location: Male urethra and lobar ducts of salivary glands | Structure: There is a layer of columnar cells present on squamous, columnar or cuboidal epithelial cells | Function: Protection and secretion

teacher_understanding.question: What makes this epithelium stratified columnar?
teacher_understanding.answer: A columnar cell layer lies above other epithelial cells, which the page says may be squamous, columnar or cuboidal.

teacher_understanding.question: Which locations are given?
teacher_understanding.answer: The male urethra and lobar ducts of salivary glands.

teacher_understanding.question: Which functions are paired?
teacher_understanding.answer: Protection and secretion.

teacher_understanding.question: How should it be distinguished from simple columnar tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Simple columnar has one cell layer. Stratified columnar has surface columnar cells above additional cells, so layer count must be checked as well as shape.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should 'male urethra' not become a claim about its entire length?
teacher_understanding.answer: Epithelial linings can change along a passage. Stratified columnar occurs in parts of the male urethra, not as a uniform lining of every part.

prerequisites: urethra as the outlet passage for urine
items.exam_note: Location matching is important. Urethra is not ureter; stratified is not pseudostratified.
